laws.title: Plurinational State Constitution
laws.subtitle: Political Constitution of the State 2009
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's 2009 constitution established the Plurinational State, recognizing 36 indigenous nations and incorporating Pachamama (Mother Earth) rights. It mandates social functions of property, nationalizes strategic resources, and enshrines autonomy for indigenous communities under the principle of 'vivir bien' (living well).
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations may lead to nullification of laws or government acts; amparo constitutional action available
exceptions: Emergency decrees subject to legislative ratification
International treaties require Assembly approval

quiz.q: What principle does Bolivia's 2009 constitution enshrine as a foundational value?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's 2009 constitution embeds 'vivir bien' — a Quechua/Aymara concept of communal harmony with nature — as a guiding principle of the Plurinational State.

laws.title: Nationalization of Hydrocarbons
laws.subtitle: Supreme Decree 28701 — May Day 2006
laws.fullDescription: President Evo Morales' 2006 nationalization decree reclaimed state control over Bolivia's oil and gas sector, requiring foreign companies to renegotiate contracts with YPFB (state oil company). Royalties and taxes on hydrocarbons rose dramatically, funding social programs. Bolivia holds South America's second-largest natural gas reserves.
laws.penalty: Operating without valid YPFB contract: expulsion and asset forfeiture
exceptions: Existing contracts renegotiated within 180 days
Joint ventures permitted with YPFB majority stake

quiz.q: Which decree nationalized Bolivia's hydrocarbons in 2006?
quiz.explanation: Supreme Decree 28701, signed on May 1, 2006 — Labor Day — nationalized Bolivia's oil and gas, becoming a defining act of Evo Morales' presidency.

laws.title: Drug Trafficking — Law 1008
laws.subtitle: Regime Applicable to Coca and Controlled Substances 1988
laws.fullDescription: Law 1008 governs coca cultivation and drug trafficking in Bolivia. It designates 'traditional' coca zones in the Yungas, permits limited cultivation for cultural and medicinal use, and criminalizes cocaine production and trafficking. Bolivia controversially withdrew from the UN Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs in 2011 over coca leaf provisions, then rejoined with a reservation on traditional use.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: 10–25 years imprisonment; coca excess: 1–5 years
exceptions: Traditional and medicinal coca use legal in designated zones
Authorized industrial coca products (mate, flour)

quiz.q: What makes Bolivia's approach to coca unique internationally?
options: It rejoined the UN Drug Convention with a reservation on traditional coca use
quiz.explanation: Bolivia rejoined the UN Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs in 2013 with a reservation protecting traditional coca leaf use — a first in international drug law.

laws.title: Law of Mother Earth
laws.subtitle: Law 071 of Mother Earth — 2010
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia enacted the world's first Law of Mother Earth (Ley de la Madre Tierra) in 2010, granting nature legal rights including the right to life, diversity, water, clean air, balance, and regeneration. The Framework Law 300 of 2012 expanded these rights and created enforcement mechanisms, reflecting indigenous Pachamama cosmology in national law.
laws.penalty: Environmental violations: fines up to BOB 500,000; criminal prosecution possible
exceptions: Traditional community land use activities
Authorized state development projects with mitigation plans

quiz.q: What was globally significant about Bolivia's Law of Mother Earth?
options: It granted legal rights to nature itself
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Law 071 was the first national law in the world to grant legal rights to nature, influenced by indigenous Pachamama beliefs and part of a global rights-of-nature movement.

laws.title: General Labor Law
laws.subtitle: Decreto Ley de 24 de mayo de 1939
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's foundational labor law establishes workers' rights including 8-hour workday, mandatory benefits (aguinaldo — 13th month bonus), vacation entitlements, severance pay (desahucio), and protection against unjustified dismissal. Amendments under Morales strengthened worker protections, and the 2009 constitution elevated labor rights to fundamental status.
laws.penalty: Labor violations: fines 1–30 minimum wages; repeated violations trigger enterprise closure
exceptions: Domestic workers under separate Law 2450
Seasonal agricultural workers subject to special regime

quiz.q: What is the 'aguinaldo' in Bolivian labor law?
options: A mandatory 13th month bonus paid at Christmas
quiz.explanation: The aguinaldo is a mandatory year-end bonus equivalent to one month's salary, required for all workers under Bolivian labor law — a key worker protection.

laws.title: Prior Consultation — TIPNIS Conflict
laws.subtitle: Law 222 and TIPNIS Territory Protection
laws.fullDescription: The TIPNIS (Isiboro Sécure National Park and Indigenous Territory) conflict erupted when the government planned a highway through protected indigenous territory. Law 180 (2011) declared TIPNIS intangible, but Law 222 (2012) required consultation, which indigenous groups rejected as a sham. The conflict highlighted tensions between development and indigenous rights under the new constitution.
laws.penalty: Violation of indigenous consultation rights: administrative nullification of projects
exceptions: National security infrastructure may proceed with modified consultation
Extractive projects subject to full prior free informed consent (CLPI)

quiz.q: What was the central legal dispute in the TIPNIS conflict?
options: Highway construction through indigenous territory without proper prior consultation
quiz.explanation: The TIPNIS conflict pitted development goals (a highway through the national park) against constitutional indigenous rights to prior, free, and informed consultation — a defining tension in Bolivian governance.

laws.title: Productive Community Social Economic Model
laws.subtitle: Law 232 — Financial Services Law 2013
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's economic model under Morales combined state capitalism with social redistribution. The Financial Services Law 2013 capped bank interest rates, mandated credit quotas for productive sectors and housing, and required banks to serve underbanked populations. Bolivia achieved remarkably low inequality and consistent growth throughout the commodity boom years.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant financial institutions: license revocation; fines up to 3% of assets
exceptions: Microfinance institutions subject to separate regulation
Foreign exchange transactions regulated by BCB

quiz.q: What did Bolivia's 2013 Financial Services Law require banks to do?
options: Cap interest rates and direct credit to productive sectors
quiz.explanation: Law 232 capped bank interest rates and required financial institutions to allocate credit quotas to housing, agriculture, and productive sectors — central to Bolivia's heterodox economic model.

laws.title: Electoral Regime Law
laws.subtitle: Law 026 — Electoral Regime 2010
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Electoral Regime Law established the Plurinational Electoral Organ (OEP), created rules for indigenous circumscriptions reserving congressional seats for native peoples, and set gender parity requirements (50% women candidates). The 2019 electoral crisis following disputed results led to Morales' resignation and interim government under Jeanine Áñez.
laws.penalty: Electoral fraud: 3–8 years imprisonment; vote-buying: 2–5 years
exceptions: International observers exempt from campaign restrictions
Indigenous community assemblies may follow traditional selection methods

quiz.q: What did Bolivia's 2019 electoral crisis result in?
options: Morales' resignation and an interim government
quiz.explanation: The 2019 disputed elections, amid OAS audit findings and mass protests, led to Morales' resignation and departure to Mexico, with interim President Jeanine Áñez taking power until 2020 elections.

laws.title: Renta Dignidad — Universal Pension
laws.subtitle: Law 3791 — 2007 Universal Pension
laws.fullDescription: Renta Dignidad (Dignity Pension) provides a universal monthly cash transfer to all Bolivians aged 60+, funded by hydrocarbon revenues. Expanded from the earlier Bonosol program, it covers approximately 900,000 elderly Bolivians. Along with Bono Juancito Pinto (school attendance) and Juana Azurduy (maternal health), it forms Bolivia's social protection framework.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent pension claims: restitution plus 3× penalty; 2–5 years imprisonment
exceptions: Recipients with existing pension may receive reduced amount
Non-resident Bolivians must register with consulate
laws.sourceLabel: Gestora Pública de la Seguridad Social

quiz.q: What funds Bolivia's Renta Dignidad universal pension?
quiz.explanation: Renta Dignidad is financed from the Direct Hydrocarbon Tax (IDH), demonstrating how Bolivia's nationalization of oil and gas resources directly funded its social programs.

laws.title: Femicide and Gender Violence Law
laws.subtitle: Law 348 — Comprehensive Law to Guarantee Women a Life Free of Violence 2013
laws.fullDescription: Law 348 created the crime of femicide (killing of a woman because of her gender) with penalties of 30 years without parole. It established specialized courts, a national registry of aggressors, and mandatory reporting. Bolivia has one of Latin America's highest rates of femicide, and implementation has been criticized as inadequate despite the law's strong provisions.
laws.penalty: Femicide: 30 years imprisonment without parole; domestic violence: 2–12 years
exceptions: Self-defense recognized as complete defense
Immediate protective orders available within 8 hours of complaint

quiz.q: What penalty does Bolivia's Law 348 impose for femicide?
quiz.explanation: Law 348 establishes 30 years imprisonment without parole for femicide, recognizing it as one of the most serious crimes — though Bolivia continues to face implementation challenges.

laws.title: Autonomy and Decentralization
laws.subtitle: Autonomy Framework Law 031 — 2010
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Autonomy Law created four levels of autonomy: departmental, regional, municipal, and indigenous-originary-peasant. It distributes fiscal resources and competencies across levels, with indigenous autonomies having the broadest self-governance rights. Conflicts between autonomy levels and national government are resolved by the Plurinational Constitutional Tribunal.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized exercise of autonomous competencies: administrative sanctions; intergovernmental disputes resolved judicially
exceptions: National security and foreign policy remain exclusive national competencies
Concurrent competencies require intergovernmental coordination agreements

quiz.q: How many levels of autonomy does Bolivia's framework recognize?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Autonomy Law 031 recognizes four sub-national levels: departmental, regional, municipal, and indigenous-originary-peasant autonomies — one of the world's most complex territorial arrangements.

laws.title: Mining and Metallurgy Law
laws.subtitle: Law 535 — 2014 Mining Code
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's 2014 Mining Law governs extraction of minerals including tin, silver, zinc, lithium, and gold. It establishes COMIBOL (state mining company) as a key actor, creates cooperative mining zones, and requires environmental impact assessments. Bolivia holds the world's largest lithium reserves in the Uyuni salt flat, making lithium law increasingly critical to national development.
laws.penalty: Illegal mining: asset forfeiture; environmental damage: criminal prosecution; 5–15 years
exceptions: Artisanal and cooperative mining under simplified regime
Indigenous community mining in traditional territories

quiz.q: What resource makes Bolivia's mining law globally significant?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia holds the world's largest known lithium reserves beneath the Salar de Uyuni — making its mining framework central to the global electric vehicle transition and energy storage industry.

laws.title: Avelino Siñani — Elizardo Pérez Education Law
laws.subtitle: Law 070 — Education Reform 2010
laws.fullDescription: Named after indigenous education pioneers, Law 070 mandated intercultural, bilingual, and decolonizing education across Bolivia. It requires teaching in indigenous languages (at least one of 36 recognized languages alongside Spanish), incorporates indigenous knowledge systems, and creates community-productive education connecting school to local productive activities. Technical education was expanded significantly.
laws.penalty: School non-compliance with bilingual mandate: administrative sanctions; inspection orders
exceptions: Urban areas with non-indigenous populations may adapt bilingual requirements
Private schools must meet national curriculum standards but may have additional subjects

quiz.q: What is distinctive about Bolivia's Education Law 070?
options: It mandated intercultural, bilingual, decolonizing education in 36 languages
It copied the French education model
quiz.explanation: Law 070 requires education in indigenous languages alongside Spanish and incorporates native knowledge systems — a radical decolonizing approach named after indigenous education pioneers Avelino Siñani and Elizardo Pérez.

laws.title: Water and Sanitation — Cochabamba Water War Legacy
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Water Rights and Law 2066
laws.fullDescription: The 2000 Cochabamba Water War — mass protests against privatization of water services — became a global symbol of resistance to water commodification. The conflict led to contract cancellation and eventually to constitutional provisions (Art. 20) guaranteeing water as a human right. Law 2066 regulates potable water services as a public good, prohibiting re-privatization.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized water privatization: contract nullification; criminal charges possible
exceptions: Community-managed water systems (EPSA) recognized under special regime
Industrial water use subject to concession from AAPS regulator

quiz.q: What event made Cochabamba, Bolivia famous in global water rights history?
options: The 2000 Water War — anti-privatization uprising that cancelled a water contract
quiz.explanation: The 2000 Cochabamba Water War saw mass protests against Bechtel's privatization of the water supply, ending in contract cancellation and influencing global water rights movements and Bolivia's constitution.

laws.title: Anti-Corruption Law — Marcelo Quiroga
laws.subtitle: Law 004 — Marcelo Quiroga Santa Cruz Anti-Corruption Law 2010
laws.fullDescription: Named after a socialist politician assassinated in the 1980 coup, Law 004 expanded anti-corruption provisions, extended statutes of limitation for corruption, enabled asset forfeiture, and created the Anti-Corruption Ministry. It controversially applies retroactively to acts committed before its enactment, raising due process concerns. High-profile cases against former President Tuto Quiroga and others were prosecuted under its provisions.
laws.penalty: Embezzlement of public funds: 5–15 years; bribing officials: 3–8 years; illicit enrichment: 5–10 years
exceptions: Voluntary disclosure before investigation reduces penalties by half
Diplomatic immunity for foreign officials

quiz.q: What is controversial about Bolivia's Law 004 anti-corruption statute?
options: It only applies to government officials
Its retroactive application to acts before its enactment
quiz.explanation: Law 004 applies retroactively to corruption acts committed before its 2010 passage — critics argue this violates the principle of non-retroactivity in criminal law, though supporters say it was needed to prosecute past impunity.

laws.title: Amazon Fires and Forest Law
laws.subtitle: Law 741 and DS 3973 — Deforestation Controversy
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Amazon and Chiquitanía regions suffered devastating fires in 2019 and subsequent years, partly attributed to Decree 3973 (2019) which expanded areas where controlled burns were permitted. Critics argued the decree accelerated deforestation; the government contended it supported small farmers. Bolivia has faced international pressure over deforestation rates that rank among South America's highest.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized forest burning: 3–8 years imprisonment; fines up to BOB 1 million per hectare
exceptions: Authorized controlled burns for agriculture in designated zones under DS 3973
Firefighters responding to emergencies exempt

quiz.q: What decree was blamed for worsening Bolivia's 2019 Amazon fires?
quiz.explanation: DS 3973 (2019) expanded zones where controlled agricultural burns were permitted. Critics linked it to the catastrophic 2019 fires that burned over 5 million hectares of Bolivia's lowlands and Amazon.

laws.title: Term Limits — Constitutional Crisis 2016
laws.subtitle: 2009 Constitution Art. 168 and 2016 Referendum
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's constitution limits presidents to two consecutive terms. After serving two terms, Evo Morales sought a third via a 2016 referendum, which he lost (51.3% NO). The Electoral Tribunal nonetheless ruled he could run again in 2019 based on a dubious Inter-American Court ruling. His 2019 electoral victory was disputed, leading to his resignation. The Constitutional Court's 2017 ruling enabling indefinite re-election was widely criticized.
laws.penalty: Unconstitutional candidacy: electoral disqualification
exceptions: First term not counted if under prior constitution (court ruling)
Transitional provisions for officials at time of 2009 constitution

quiz.q: How did Morales attempt to circumvent Bolivia's two-term presidential limit?
options: Won a referendum allowing re-election (which he actually lost)
Had the Electoral Tribunal rule his first terms didn't count under new constitution
quiz.explanation: After losing a 2016 referendum on term limits (51.3% NO), Morales used a Constitutional Tribunal ruling claiming his terms under the old constitution didn't count — allowing him to run in 2019, contributing to the electoral crisis.

laws.title: Universal Health Insurance — SUS
laws.subtitle: Law 1152 — Universal Health System 2019
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Universal Health System (SUS), enacted in 2019, extended free healthcare to all Bolivians not covered by social security insurance — approximately 6.5 million people. Services include primary care, specialty consultations, hospitalization, surgeries, and medicines. Funded by the state, SUS represented a major expansion of the right to health enshrined in the 2009 constitution.
laws.penalty: Healthcare providers denying SUS coverage: administrative sanctions; patient complaints to SEDES
exceptions: Private health services remain available and regulated separately
Social security (CNS) enrollees use different system but can access SUS for uncovered services

quiz.q: Approximately how many previously uninsured Bolivians did the 2019 SUS universal health law cover?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Universal Health System (SUS) extended free healthcare to approximately 6.5 million Bolivians not covered by employment-linked social security — a major expansion of constitutional health rights.

laws.title: Coca Leaf Industrialization
laws.subtitle: Law 906 — General Coca Law 2017
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's 2017 General Coca Law expanded legal coca cultivation from 12,000 to 22,000 hectares, recognized coca as a cultural heritage crop, and mandated YPFB-style industrialization of coca for export. Products including coca flour, tea, toothpaste, and energizing drinks have been promoted internationally. Bolivia has pushed to remove coca leaf from the UN's list of controlled substances.
laws.penalty: Excess cultivation beyond authorized zones: eradication; trafficking of coca paste: 10–25 years
exceptions: Traditional coca chewing (acullico) is a constitutionally protected right
Yungas and Chapare traditional zones have different cultivation limits

quiz.q: What did Bolivia's 2017 Coca Law change regarding cultivation limits?
options: Increased legal cultivation from 12,000 to 22,000 hectares
quiz.explanation: Law 906 increased legal coca cultivation from 12,000 to 22,000 hectares, reflecting a shift toward industrialization of coca products and Bolivia's push for international acceptance of coca leaf uses.

laws.title: Coup and Political Violence — Áñez Prosecution
laws.subtitle: Penal Code Arts. 121-123 — Sedition and Terrorism
laws.fullDescription: Following Bolivia's 2019 political crisis, interim President Jeanine Áñez and her ministers were prosecuted for 'sedition, terrorism, and conspiracy' relating to her assumption of power. Áñez was sentenced to 10 years in a trial that international observers and the Inter-American Commission criticized as politically motivated. The case highlighted deep polarization and concerns about judicial independence in Bolivia.
laws.penalty: Coup/sedition: 15–30 years; terrorism: 25–30 years; conspiracy: 8–15 years
exceptions: Constitutional succession in cases of vacancy is protected
De facto government measures are invalidated, not criminalized per se

quiz.q: What was Jeanine Áñez convicted of in Bolivia in 2022?
options: Sedition (in connection with her 2019 assumption of the presidency)
quiz.explanation: Áñez was convicted of sedition and other charges relating to her 2019 assumption of Bolivia's presidency after Morales' resignation — a verdict criticized by the IACHR and opposition as politically motivated.

laws.title: Bolivianization — Currency Policy
laws.subtitle: BCB Policy and DS 28899 — 2006
laws.fullDescription: 'Bolivianization' refers to Bolivia's successful policy of reducing dollar holdings in favor of bolivianos. After 2006, through favorable exchange rates and regulatory incentives, the share of bank deposits in bolivianos rose from under 10% to over 90% by 2015. This gave the central bank greater monetary sovereignty. However, Bolivia's near-depletion of foreign reserves by 2023-2024 created a new currency crisis.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized foreign exchange dealing: fines and license revocation
exceptions: International trade contracts may be denominated in foreign currency
Foreign investment remittances protected by investment treaties

quiz.q: What did Bolivia's 'bolivianization' policy achieve?
options: Pegged the boliviano to the US dollar
Reduced dollar deposits from ~90% to under 10% of bank deposits
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's bolivianization policy reversed extreme dollarization — increasing boliviano deposits from under 10% to over 90% of bank deposits, restoring monetary sovereignty until a foreign reserve crisis emerged circa 2023-24.

laws.title: Indigenous Justice Systems
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Art. 190-192 and Law 073 — Jurisdictional Deslinde 2010
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's constitution recognizes indigenous justice systems (justicia indígena originaria campesina) as equal to the ordinary justice system. Law 073 (Deslinde Jurisdiccional) delineates competencies: indigenous courts handle matters within their territory, culture, and members, but cannot override rights to life or prohibit cruel punishment. Coordination mechanisms between systems have been slow to develop.
laws.penalty: Violation of indigenous jurisdiction by ordinary courts: nullification of acts; intergovernmental complaints mechanism
exceptions: Crimes against humanity, femicide, child abuse, and trafficking remain in ordinary jurisdiction
Rights to life and prohibition of torture cannot be overridden

quiz.q: What does Bolivia's Law 073 regulate?
options: The boundary between indigenous justice and ordinary courts
quiz.explanation: Law 073 (Deslinde Jurisdiccional) delineates which matters fall under indigenous justice systems vs. ordinary courts — a complex interface required by Bolivia's constitutional recognition of dual legal systems.

laws.title: Migration Law
laws.subtitle: Law 370 — Migration Law 2013
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Migration Law 370 establishes rights of migrants, including access to education, healthcare, and social services regardless of status. Bolivia signed agreements with Mercosur and Andean Community countries allowing free residency. The law prohibits deportation without due process and recognizes the right to family unity. Significant Bolivian communities live in Argentina, Brazil, Spain, and the United States.
laws.penalty: Human trafficking: 8–12 years; unauthorized border crossing: administrative fine, not criminal
exceptions: MERCOSUR and CAN nationals receive expedited residency
Asylum seekers and refugees under separate CONARE regime

quiz.q: How does Bolivia treat undocumented border crossing under Law 370?
options: Administrative fine only, not a criminal matter
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Migration Law 370 treats unauthorized border crossing as an administrative infraction subject to fines rather than a criminal offense — a relatively liberal approach to migration enforcement.

laws.title: Lithium Industrialization Law
laws.subtitle: Law 928 — YPFB Lithium Strategy and YLB
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia created Yacimientos de Litio Bolivianos (YLB) in 2017 to industrialize its lithium reserves at Salar de Uyuni — estimated at 21 million tonnes (world's largest). The strategy aims to move beyond raw material export to producing batteries and electric vehicles domestically. International partnerships have been controversial, including a German company agreement and a Chinese CATL deal. Bolivia's lithium nationalization aims to replicate the oil nationalization model.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized lithium extraction: criminal prosecution; contracts void ab initio
exceptions: Research projects with academic institutions may have access under MOU
Joint ventures with YLB majority control permitted under law

quiz.q: What is Bolivia's goal for its lithium resources beyond raw extraction?
options: Produce batteries and electric vehicles domestically to add industrial value
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's YLB strategy aims to industrialize lithium — moving from raw salt extraction to battery cell and electric vehicle production domestically, replicating the value-capture model of oil nationalization.

laws.title: Plurinational Constitutional Tribunal
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Art. 196-204 and Law 027 TCP
laws.fullDescription: The Plurinational Constitutional Tribunal (TCP) is Bolivia's supreme constitutional court, unique in that its members are elected by popular vote rather than appointed — the only court in the world chosen this way. Critics argue judicial elections politicize the judiciary; supporters say it democratizes justice. The TCP rules on constitutionality of laws, resolves jurisdictional conflicts between autonomy levels, and hears individual rights actions.
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations: nullification of laws; amparo tutela actions for individual rights; 30-day resolution deadline for urgent cases
exceptions: Political questions doctrine limits review of purely political acts
International treaty obligations create interpretive presumptions

quiz.q: What makes Bolivia's Constitutional Tribunal uniquely democratic?
options: Its members are elected by popular vote — unique in the world
It can be dissolved by referendum
It has no judicial review power
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's TCP members are elected by popular vote — the only constitutional court in the world chosen this way. This radical democratization of justice is celebrated by some and criticized as politicizing the judiciary.

laws.title: Bono Juancito Pinto — Education Conditional Transfer
laws.subtitle: DS 28899 — 2006 School Attendance Bonus
laws.fullDescription: Bono Juancito Pinto provides an annual cash transfer (BOB 200 per year) to families who keep children enrolled in public school through sixth grade, later expanded to secondary school. Named after a child mascot of the 1879 War of the Pacific, it has been credited with dramatic increases in school attendance and reduction of child labor. Over 2 million students receive it annually.
laws.penalty: False enrollment claims: restitution of full amount plus 50% penalty; educational institution sanctions
exceptions: Students in private schools ineligible
Children with documented disabilities may receive regardless of attendance metrics

quiz.q: What behavior does Bolivia's Bono Juancito Pinto incentivize?
options: Keeping children enrolled in public school
quiz.explanation: Bono Juancito Pinto is a conditional cash transfer paid to families who maintain their children's enrollment in public school — credited with major increases in school attendance and reduction of child labor across Bolivia.

laws.title: Preventive Detention — CAICOR Reform
laws.subtitle: Law 1173 — Abbreviation of Criminal Proceedings 2019
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia has among Latin America's highest rates of preventive detention — historically over 70% of prisoners awaiting trial. Law 1173 (2019) sought to reduce this by limiting reasons for preventive detention, capping pre-trial detention duration, expanding alternative measures, and requiring faster case processing. Critics noted implementation has been slow and prison overcrowding continues to be severe.
laws.penalty: Illegal detention by officials: 2–5 years; failure to process cases timely: disciplinary sanctions
exceptions: Preventive detention still permitted for flight risk or evidence tampering
Serious crimes (terrorism, drug trafficking) have extended detention limits

quiz.q: What was Bolivia's historic rate of prisoners in preventive (pre-trial) detention?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia historically had over 70% of its prisoners in preventive detention awaiting trial — one of Latin America's highest rates — prompting Law 1173 to limit pre-trial detention and speed case processing.

laws.title: Food Sovereignty Law
laws.subtitle: Law 144 — Productive Communitarian Agricultural Revolution 2011
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's food sovereignty law (Law 144) promotes indigenous seed systems, restricts GMO crop authorization, supports campesino (small farmer) production, and links agricultural policy to indigenous worldviews. Bolivia has been inconsistent on GMOs, with government allowing some approvals for soy and maize while maintaining official anti-GMO rhetoric, reflecting tensions between agribusiness interests and food sovereignty principles.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized GMO crops: seizure and destruction; non-compliance with seed law: fines and bans
exceptions: Research institutions may work with GMO material under controlled conditions
Existing approved GMO varieties have transitional permits

quiz.q: What tension exists in Bolivia's food sovereignty law regarding GMOs?
options: No tension — it fully bans all GMOs
It fully embraces GMOs for export
Official anti-GMO law coexists with government approvals of some GMO crops for agribusiness
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Law 144 restricts GMOs in principle, but the government has approved GMO soy and maize varieties — creating a gap between food sovereignty rhetoric and agribusiness reality in the country's agricultural policy.

laws.title: Sacaba and Senkata Massacres — State Violence Law
laws.subtitle: Penal Code Arts. 138-139 and Criminal Investigation
laws.fullDescription: During Bolivia's 2019 political crisis, security forces killed at least 10 protesters in Sacaba (November 15) and 9 in Senkata (November 19) under interim President Áñez. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights condemned the killings. Investigations and prosecutions followed, with some military and police officers charged. The cases raised questions about command responsibility and the use of force.
laws.penalty: Extrajudicial killing by state agents: 20–30 years; command responsibility if ordered: 25–30 years
exceptions: Proportionate use of force in response to imminent threat is a defense
Following lawful orders is a partial defense unless order is manifestly illegal
laws.sourceLabel: CIDH — Inter-American Commission on Human Rights

quiz.q: How many protesters were killed in the Sacaba and Senkata incidents during Bolivia's 2019 crisis?
quiz.explanation: Security forces killed at least 19 protesters total — 10 in Sacaba and 9 in Senkata — during the 2019 political crisis under interim President Áñez, drawing IACHR condemnation and criminal investigations.

laws.title: Economic Crisis — Fuel Subsidies and Reserve Depletion
laws.subtitle: DS 21060 Legacy and 2023-2024 Fiscal Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's neoliberal DS 21060 (1985) ended hyperinflation but devastated labor and state industries. Under Morales, massive fuel subsidies became entrenched. By 2023-24, Bolivia faced foreign reserve depletion (reportedly under $400 million), fuel shortages, and currency crisis as hydrocarbon revenues declined and subsidy costs soared. The IMF and economists warned of unsustainability; Bolivia sought emergency financing.
laws.penalty: Black market fuel trading: fines and criminal prosecution; foreign currency speculation: up to 5 years
exceptions: Emergency fuel imports authorized under executive decree
Central bank emergency measures under BCB Act

quiz.q: What caused Bolivia's 2023-24 economic crisis?
options: Depletion of foreign reserves as hydrocarbon revenues declined while fuel subsidies remained high
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's 2023-24 crisis stemmed from depleted foreign reserves — a result of declining natural gas revenues combined with massive, politically entrenched fuel subsidies that the government could no longer sustain.

laws.title: Plurinational Assembly Structure
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Arts. 145-162
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Plurinational Legislative Assembly consists of the Chamber of Deputies (130 members) and Senate (36 members). Unique features include 7 reserved seats for indigenous minorities in the Chamber, gender parity requirements, and representation of indigenous nations. The Assembly has broad powers including approving the national budget, ratifying international treaties, and declaring states of emergency.
laws.penalty: Failure to observe quorum or procedural rules: sessions voided; fines for unexcused absences
exceptions: Urgent legislative procedures allow accelerated processing for emergency laws
Presidential decrees during recess subject to ratification

quiz.q: How many reserved seats do indigenous minorities have in Bolivia's Chamber of Deputies?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's constitution reserves 7 seats in the 130-member Chamber of Deputies specifically for indigenous minority nations — ensuring representation for the smallest native groups beyond the general indigenous quota.

laws.title: Arms and Ammunition Control
laws.subtitle: Law 400 — Arms and Ammunition 2013
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Arms Law restricts civilian firearm ownership, requires registration and licensing, prohibits military-grade weapons for civilians, and mandates safe storage. The law was strengthened amid concerns about narco-trafficking weapons and political violence. Bolivia cooperates with UNODC on weapons tracing and has participated in arms buyback programs.
laws.penalty: Illegal possession: 3–8 years; trafficking: 10–25 years; using in crime: sentence enhancement
exceptions: Licensed security guards may carry registered sidearms
Rural residents may hold hunting rifles under simplified registration

quiz.q: What drove tightening of Bolivia's Arms Law 400?
options: Concerns about narco-trafficking weapons and political violence
quiz.explanation: Bolivia tightened arms control amid concerns about weapons linked to drug trafficking organizations and political violence — cooperating with UNODC on weapons tracing and buyback programs.

laws.title: Cooperatives Law
laws.subtitle: Law 356 — General Cooperatives Law 2013
laws.fullDescription: Cooperatives play a major role in Bolivia's economy, particularly in mining, where cooperatives extract significant portions of minerals. Law 356 regulates cooperative formation, governance, profit distribution, and labor rights of members. Mining cooperatives have been controversial — sometimes operating under favorable terms that critics say compete unfairly with unionized workers, and occasionally involved in violent conflicts over mining rights.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent cooperative formation: dissolution; labor rights violations within cooperatives: same as employer violations
exceptions: Agricultural cooperatives have simplified registration
Social solidarity economy cooperatives may receive tax benefits

quiz.q: In which sector are cooperatives most controversially significant in Bolivia?
options: Mining — where they extract major mineral quantities under favorable terms
quiz.explanation: Mining cooperatives in Bolivia control significant mineral extraction and have long been controversial — benefiting from favorable regulatory treatment while sometimes resisting labor standards applied to corporate mines.

laws.title: Lake Titicaca Protection
laws.subtitle: Bolivia-Peru Binational Authority TDPS
laws.fullDescription: Lake Titicaca, the world's highest navigable lake at 3,810m, is shared by Bolivia and Peru and protected under a binational authority (TDPS). Bolivia's Environmental Law and international agreements regulate pollution, overfishing, and invasive species in the lake. The 2018 fish kill — caused by pollution and eutrophication — killed thousands of fish and frogs, prompting emergency environmental response.
laws.penalty: Illegal dumping into Lake Titicaca: criminal prosecution; fines up to BOB 2 million
exceptions: Traditional fishing communities have ancestral rights under indigenous law
Scientific research with environmental permits

quiz.q: What is unusual about Lake Titicaca's governance structure?
options: It is governed by a private company
It is managed by a Bolivia-Peru binational authority (TDPS)
quiz.explanation: Lake Titicaca is governed by the binational Bolivia-Peru Autonomous Authority of Lake Titicaca (TDPS) — one of few internationally shared water bodies with a dedicated joint management institution.

laws.title: Child Protection — Code Niña, Niño, Adolescente
laws.subtitle: Law 548 — Children and Adolescents Code 2014
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Children and Adolescents Code 2014 establishes comprehensive child protection, including minimum age of criminal responsibility (14), juvenile justice system, protection from abuse, and provisions for street children. Controversially, the code originally allowed children as young as 10 to work in family enterprises — revised after international criticism — reflecting the practical reality of widespread child labor in Bolivia.
laws.penalty: Child abuse: 8–15 years; sexual exploitation of minors: 15–20 years; worst forms of child labor: 5–10 years
exceptions: Cultural community activities with parental consent recognized
Educational work experience for adolescents 14+ with labor authority approval
laws.sourceLabel: Defensorías de la Niñez y Adolescencia Bolivia

quiz.q: What controversial provision did Bolivia's 2014 Children Code originally include?
options: Allowing children from age 10 to work in family enterprises
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Children Code 2014 controversially permitted children from age 10 to work in family enterprises — revised after international criticism from ILO and UNICEF, reflecting the practical reality of widespread child labor in Bolivia.

laws.title: Productive Economic Community Model
laws.subtitle: Law 466 — EPNE and State Enterprises 2013
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia established a framework for Strategic Public National Enterprises (EPNE) under Law 466, converting nationalized companies into commercially viable state enterprises. YPFB (oil), ENTEL (telecom), BOA (airline), ENDE (electricity), and others operate under this framework. The model aims to generate profits for social programs while maintaining state control over strategic sectors.
laws.penalty: State enterprise corruption or mismanagement: Criminal Code plus Law 004 anti-corruption; 5–15 years
exceptions: EPNEs may form joint ventures without losing state character
Emergency operational decisions exempt from normal procurement

quiz.q: Name one of Bolivia's key strategic state enterprises under Law 466.
quiz.explanation: YPFB (Yacimientos Petrolíferos Fiscales Bolivianos) is Bolivia's state oil company and most important EPNE — generating revenues that fund social programs like Renta Dignidad and Bono Juancito Pinto.

laws.title: Freedom of Expression — Media Law
laws.subtitle: Law 164 — Telecommunications and ICT 2011
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's telecommunications law regulates broadcast media licensing, spectrum allocation, and digital content. Press freedom organizations have raised concerns about government pressure on private media, concentration of state media, and criminal defamation provisions. The Morales government was particularly criticized for using regulatory powers to pressure critical outlets, and several journalists were prosecuted under defamation laws.
laws.penalty: Criminal defamation: 1–3 years; incitement through media: 3–5 years; unauthorized broadcasting: fines and closure
exceptions: Journalistic investigations on matters of public interest have heightened protection
Community radio stations under simplified licensing

quiz.q: What concern has press freedom organizations raised about Bolivia's media environment?
options: Government use of regulatory powers to pressure critical media outlets
quiz.explanation: Press freedom groups have documented the Bolivian government's use of spectrum licensing, advertising withdrawal, and defamation prosecutions to pressure critical private media — a pattern seen across multiple administrations.

laws.title: Chiquitanía and Pantanal Protection
laws.subtitle: Forestry Law 1700 and Environmental Framework
laws.fullDescription: The Chiquitanía dry forest and Bolivia's portion of the Pantanal wetland (world's largest tropical wetland) require special protection under Bolivia's Forest Law 1700 and environmental regulations. Cattle ranching expansion, fires, and agribusiness have threatened these ecosystems. Bolivia's 2019 fires were particularly devastating in the Chiquitanía, burning over 4 million hectares.
laws.penalty: Deforestation in protected Chiquitanía zones: fines up to BOB 500/hectare plus reforestation obligation; criminal charges for repeat offenders
exceptions: Existing ranching titles in transition zones have grandfather provisions
Emergency fire breaks authorized for fire control
laws.sourceLabel: Autoridad de Bosques y Tierra Bolivia

quiz.q: What ecosystem is the Pantanal, part of which Bolivia shares?
quiz.explanation: The Pantanal is the world's largest tropical wetland, spanning Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay. Bolivia's portion requires specific protection under forest and environmental laws, threatened by fires and agricultural expansion.

laws.title: Rights of Persons with Disabilities
laws.subtitle: Law 223 — Comprehensive Law for Persons with Disabilities 2012
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's disability law (Law 223) provides comprehensive rights and social protection for persons with disabilities, including employment quotas (4% in public entities), free healthcare, priority attention, and subsidies. The law gained international attention when former President Evo Morales himself has a disability — and because disabled protesters (los discapacitados) conducted dramatic marches from Cochabamba to La Paz demanding better support.
laws.penalty: Discrimination against disabled persons: fines 1–5 minimum wages; denial of employment quota: administrative sanctions
exceptions: Small enterprises under 10 employees exempt from employment quotas
Emergency situations may delay accessibility modifications

quiz.q: What famous long-distance protest did disabled Bolivians conduct?
options: Dramatic marches from Cochabamba to La Paz demanding better disability support
Chaining themselves to the Presidential Palace
quiz.explanation: Disabled Bolivians conducted multiple grueling marches from Cochabamba to La Paz (400+ km), demanding improved disability benefits — compelling media attention and policy negotiations despite harsh conditions.

laws.title: Nationalization of Electricity — ENDE
laws.subtitle: Law 466 and DS 1135 — ENDE Nationalization
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia nationalized electricity distribution companies in 2012, bringing them under ENDE (Empresa Nacional de Electricidad). The country has achieved high electrification rates (over 90%) and invested heavily in hydroelectric capacity. Bolivia also exports electricity to neighboring countries. The energy matrix relies heavily on natural gas for thermal generation, with growing renewable capacity.
laws.penalty: Illegal operation of electricity infrastructure: criminal prosecution; operating without AETN license: fines and closure
exceptions: Community micro-hydro projects under 1MW have simplified licensing
Solar off-grid systems for rural isolated communities under PRONER program

quiz.q: What has Bolivia achieved with its nationalized electricity system?
options: Over 90% electrification rate with significant hydroelectric capacity
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's nationalized ENDE electricity company has achieved over 90% electrification nationwide and developed significant hydroelectric capacity, also exporting power to neighbors — a success of the state enterprise model.

laws.title: Human Trafficking Law
laws.subtitle: Law 263 — Comprehensive Anti-Trafficking Law 2012
laws.fullDescription: Law 263 criminalizes human trafficking and migrant smuggling with heavy penalties. Bolivia is a source, transit, and destination country for trafficking, particularly for labor exploitation in Argentina's textile industry and sexual exploitation. The law created specialized trafficking courts and required training for judiciary, police, and social workers. Coordination with Argentina and Brazil on cross-border trafficking has improved.
laws.penalty: Human trafficking: 8–12 years; trafficking of minors: 10–15 years; organized trafficking: 12–20 years
exceptions: Victims of trafficking receive immunity from immigration offenses
Witness protection available for trafficking victims who cooperate with prosecution

quiz.q: In which country's textile industry have Bolivian trafficking victims frequently been exploited?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia is a major source of trafficking victims for Argentina's textile industry (particularly in Buenos Aires), where Bolivians have been found in debt bondage in clandestine workshops — prompting bilateral cooperation.

laws.title: ALBA and Trade Diplomacy
laws.subtitle: ALBA-TCP and Bolivia's Alternative Trade Agreements
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia joined ALBA (Bolivarian Alliance for the Americas) under Morales, participating in Venezuela's oil-for-services programs and Cuba's medical missions. Bolivia has trade agreements with the Andean Community (CAN), MERCOSUR as associate member, and bilateral agreements with Brazil, Argentina, and China. After Morales, Bolivia maintained most trade relationships while reducing ALBA emphasis.
laws.penalty: Trade agreement violations subject to dispute resolution mechanisms; non-compliant imports: customs penalties
exceptions: ALBA medical cooperation continues under separate humanitarian framework
CAN rules of origin apply to preferential tariff access

quiz.q: What did Bolivia receive from Venezuela through ALBA?
quiz.explanation: Through ALBA, Bolivia received Venezuelan oil on preferential terms and Cuban medical missions that provided healthcare in underserved areas — part of Morales' '21st century socialism' international alignments.

laws.title: Social Housing Program — Mi Teleférico
laws.subtitle: Urban Transport and Housing Policy
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia built La Paz's Mi Teleférico (My Cable Car) — the world's longest urban cable car system — as part of integrated urban transport and development policy. Covering over 30km and 10 lines, it connects La Paz and El Alto across dramatic Andean terrain. The project became a symbol of Morales' development vision, though criticized for cost and underutilization of some lines. Housing programs also expanded under FONVIS and housing bonds.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent housing subsidy applications: restitution plus penalties; construction violations: project suspension
exceptions: Social housing near cable car stations received priority allocation
Emergency housing after disasters under simplified procedures

quiz.q: What infrastructure achievement made Bolivia internationally recognized in urban transport?
options: Mi Teleférico — world's longest urban cable car system connecting La Paz and El Alto
quiz.explanation: Mi Teleférico in La Paz-El Alto is the world's longest and highest urban cable car system — a bold solution to connecting cities at vastly different altitudes across the challenging Andean terrain.

laws.title: Intelligence Services Law
laws.subtitle: Law 1009 — Intelligence and Counter-Intelligence 2017
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Intelligence Law regulates the National Intelligence System, restricts surveillance of civilians, and requires judicial authorization for wiretapping. Under Morales, intelligence services were accused of monitoring political opponents, journalists, and NGOs. The law attempts to balance security needs with civil liberties protections, though oversight remains weak according to human rights monitors.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized surveillance: 3–8 years; disclosure of classified intelligence: 5–10 years
exceptions: Counter-terrorism investigations may access communications metadata with prosecutor authorization
Foreign intelligence sharing under bilateral security agreements

quiz.q: What restriction does Bolivia's Intelligence Law place on surveillance?
options: Only military personnel can be monitored
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Law 1009 requires judicial authorization for wiretapping and surveillance of civilians — though implementation and oversight have been criticized as inadequate by human rights organizations.

laws.title: Telecommunications and Internet Access
laws.subtitle: Law 164 — General Telecommunications 2011
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Telecommunications Law created the ATT regulator, established universal service obligations for rural access, and declared internet access a basic right. ENTEL (state telecom) was nationalized in 2008 and plays a dominant role. Bolivia launched TUPAC KATARI — its own communications satellite in 2013 — reducing dependence on foreign satellite services and enabling rural connectivity.
laws.penalty: Operating without ATT license: fines up to BOB 500,000; data privacy violations: fines and license suspension
exceptions: Community radio and rural telephony under simplified regime
Emergency communications during disasters exempt from normal procedure

quiz.q: What space achievement did Bolivia accomplish in 2013 to support connectivity?
options: Launched TUPAC KATARI — Bolivia's first communications satellite
quiz.explanation: Bolivia launched its first communications satellite TUPAC KATARI in 2013, named after an 18th-century indigenous leader — enabling rural connectivity and reducing dependence on foreign satellite services.

laws.title: Fisheries and Amazonian Biodiversity
laws.subtitle: Environmental Framework and Amazon Biodiversity Law
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Amazon basin harbors extraordinary biodiversity, with the Madeira, Beni, and Mamoré river systems supporting endemic species. Fishing regulations protect endemic species like the dorado catfish (a large migratory species), and environmental laws protect the broader Amazonian ecosystem. Climate change and deforestation threaten biodiversity, and Bolivia participates in the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO).
laws.penalty: Illegal fishing of protected species: fines and equipment confiscation; environmental damage to Amazon: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Indigenous subsistence fishing rights protected under Law 073
Scientific research with SERNAP permits

quiz.q: What treaty organization does Bolivia participate in for Amazon cooperation?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia is a member of ACTO (Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization), which promotes sustainable development and environmental protection across all eight Amazon basin countries including Brazil, Peru, and Colombia.

laws.title: Sea Access Claim Against Chile
laws.subtitle: Bolivia's Landlocked Status and ICJ Case
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia lost its Pacific coast to Chile in the 1884 War of the Pacific and has campaigned for sea access ever since. In 2013, Bolivia filed a case before the International Court of Justice arguing Chile had an obligation to negotiate sea access. In 2018, the ICJ ruled it had jurisdiction but ultimately ruled in Chile's favor in the merits — finding no legal obligation on Chile to negotiate. Bolivia's sea claim remains a central national aspiration.
laws.penalty: N/A — international diplomatic and legal dispute
exceptions: Bolivia does have transit rights through Chilean ports under bilateral treaties
Free trade zone in Iquique used by Bolivia under special arrangements

quiz.q: What was the ICJ's 2018 ruling in Bolivia's sea access case against Chile?
options: Awarded Bolivia a corridor to the sea
Found Chile had a legal obligation to negotiate
Ruled in Chile's favor — no legal obligation to negotiate sea access
quiz.explanation: The ICJ ruled in 2018 that Chile has no legal obligation under international law to negotiate sovereign sea access with Bolivia — a major blow to Bolivia's 130+ year diplomatic campaign to regain its coast.

laws.title: Terrorism and Civic Committee Investigations
laws.subtitle: Penal Code Arts. 123-126 and 2019 Prosecution
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's terrorism laws were applied controversially in 2020-2021 against civic and opposition figures accused of participating in the 2019 political crisis. 'Civic Committee' leaders from Santa Cruz — who led strikes and protests against Morales — faced terrorism charges that international observers criticized as political persecution. The cases highlighted how broad terrorism definitions can be misused against political opponents.
laws.penalty: Terrorism: 25–30 years; financing terrorism: 15–20 years; association with terrorist organization: 10–15 years
exceptions: Legitimate civil disobedience and protest protected under constitution
Broad political strike is not terrorism per ILO standards

quiz.q: How were Bolivia's terrorism laws controversial in 2020-2021?
options: They were too lenient on actual terrorists
Applied against civic leaders from Santa Cruz who led anti-Morales protests in 2019
quiz.explanation: The Arce government applied terrorism charges against Santa Cruz civic leaders who had led 2019 anti-Morales protests — a use of broad terrorism definitions that international observers criticized as political prosecution.

laws.title: Beef Export Policy — Santa Cruz Agribusiness
laws.subtitle: Agricultural Export Regulation and DS 4749
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Santa Cruz department is a major agribusiness hub, producing soy, cattle, and sugarcane. Export policies for beef have fluctuated between promotion (to earn foreign exchange) and restriction (to control domestic prices). Bolivia has sought to expand beef exports to China, which became Bolivia's top trading partner. Soy exports to Brazil, Argentina, and China represent major foreign exchange earnings.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized beef exports during price control periods: fines up to 100% of export value
exceptions: Small-scale cross-border informal trade has tolerance thresholds
Organic and premium beef under separate export protocols

quiz.q: Which country became Bolivia's top trading partner for agribusiness exports?
quiz.explanation: China became Bolivia's largest trading partner, importing Bolivian beef, soybeans, and other agribusiness products — and is a key financier of Bolivian infrastructure and lithium development projects.

laws.title: Foreign Policy — Non-Alignment and Anti-Imperialism
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Arts. 255-258 and Bolivian Foreign Policy
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's 2009 constitution establishes foreign policy principles including rejection of imperialism, US military bases, and nuclear weapons, and promotion of South-South cooperation. Under Morales, Bolivia expelled the US DEA, US Ambassador (briefly), and USAID, accusing them of interference. Relations with Venezuela, Cuba, Iran, and Russia were cultivated, while relations with the US remained tense.
laws.penalty: Foreign interference in Bolivian affairs: constitutional basis for expulsion; treaty violations subject to diplomatic remedies
exceptions: UN peacekeeping commitments continue regardless of political alignments
Bilateral investment treaties remain in force despite political tensions

quiz.q: Which international organization did Bolivia expel from its territory under Evo Morales?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia expelled the US DEA in 2008, accusing it of interference in sovereign drug policy — following President Morales's own background as a coca growers' union leader and his rejection of US coca eradication demands.

laws.title: University Autonomy and Free Education
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Art. 91 and Ley Universitaria
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's universities enjoy constitutionally guaranteed autonomy — self-governance in academic, administrative, and economic matters. Public university education is free. The major state universities (UMSA in La Paz, UMSS in Cochabamba) are co-governed by students and faculty. University reform movements have historically driven broader social change in Bolivia, including the 1952 Revolution.
laws.penalty: Government interference in university autonomy: unconstitutional; academic fraud: institutional disciplinary action
exceptions: Federal budget oversight of public university spending is permitted
Private universities must meet national accreditation standards (CEUB)

quiz.q: Who co-governs Bolivia's public universities under the university autonomy system?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's public universities are co-governed by students and faculty (co-gobierno universitario) — a form of academic democracy protected by constitutional autonomy that dates to the 1918 Córdoba Reform movement across Latin America.

laws.title: Cocaine Transit and Interdiction
laws.subtitle: Law 1008 Enforcement and FELCN Operations
laws.fullDescription: Despite Bolivia's nationalist coca policy, the country remains a significant cocaine producer and transit hub. The Anti-Drug Police Force (FELCN) conducts interdiction operations. Bolivia has cooperated with Brazil and Europe on trafficking routes while resisting US-led eradication pressure. The Chapare coca region remains contested, with Morales' coca growers unions often in tension with anti-drug operations.
laws.penalty: Cocaine production: 10–25 years; trafficking: 15–25 years; drug money laundering: 8–15 years
exceptions: Authorized coca cultivation under Law 1008 not criminalized
Medical marijuana research permitted under strict controls

quiz.q: What is FELCN in Bolivia?
options: The Anti-Drug Police Force conducting cocaine interdiction
quiz.explanation: FELCN (Fuerza Especial de Lucha Contra el Narcotráfico) is Bolivia's specialized anti-drug police force, conducting cocaine seizures and interdiction operations — operating alongside competing political pressures from coca union interests.

laws.title: Glacial Retreat and Climate Adaptation
laws.subtitle: Chacaltaya and Andean Water Security
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Chacaltaya glacier — once the world's highest ski resort at 5,421m — disappeared entirely by 2009. Andean glaciers provide critical dry-season water for La Paz, Oruro, and Cochabamba. Bolivia declared a 'water emergency' in 2016 when drought and glacial retreat threatened La Paz's water supply. Climate adaptation plans include reservoir construction and alternative water sources.
laws.penalty: Violation of water emergency restrictions: fines and criminal charges
exceptions: Emergency military engineering for water infrastructure authorized
International climate finance projects exempt from standard procurement
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Medio Ambiente y Agua Bolivia

quiz.q: What happened to Bolivia's Chacaltaya glacier?
options: It grew due to climate change
It was converted to a ski resort
quiz.explanation: Chacaltaya — once the world's highest ski resort — disappeared entirely by 2009 due to climate change. The loss of Andean glaciers threatens dry-season water supplies for millions of Bolivians in La Paz, Cochabamba, and Oruro.

laws.title: Lustration and Historical Memory
laws.subtitle: Law 879 — Day of Memory Against Coups and Political Violence 2016
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's varied history of military coups (over 190 in its history — more per year than any other country) has led to laws recognizing victims of political violence. Law 879 established March 22 as the Day of Memory. The Marcelo Quiroga Santa Cruz Reconciliation Law addressed abuses from the 1971-1978 Banzer dictatorship and the 1980 García Meza coup. Reparations for victims remain incomplete.
laws.penalty: New acts of coups: treason and sedition charges; destroying historical documentation: criminal offense
exceptions: Truth commission findings may lead to reduced penalties for voluntary disclosure
Pardons for minor coup participants considered after democratic transition

quiz.q: What is Bolivia infamous for regarding its political history?
options: Having over 190 coups — more per capita per year than almost any other country
Being the first Latin American democracy
quiz.explanation: Bolivia has experienced over 190 coups and coup attempts — giving it one of the world's highest rates of political interruption per year, reflecting its complex history of military interventions and political instability.

laws.title: Traditional Medicine — Kallawaya
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Recognition and Intercultural Health
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia constitutionally recognizes traditional medicine alongside Western medicine. The Kallawaya — itinerant herbalists from the Bolivian highlands — are UNESCO-recognized bearers of intangible cultural heritage. Bolivia's intercultural health policy integrates traditional healing with the formal health system, particularly for indigenous communities. The 'Model of Family, Community, and Intercultural Health' (SAFCI) was a key Morales-era innovation.
laws.penalty: Practicing traditional medicine without registration: administrative fines
exceptions: Kallawaya and recognized traditional practitioners exempt from pharmacy regulations
Indigenous community healing ceremonies protected under constitutional plurinationalism

quiz.q: What are the Kallawaya recognized for internationally?
options: UNESCO-recognized itinerant herbalists — bearers of intangible cultural heritage
quiz.explanation: The Kallawaya are itinerant herbalists from Bolivia's highlands recognized by UNESCO as bearers of intangible cultural heritage — their knowledge of medicinal plants spans centuries and is constitutionally protected.

laws.title: Territorial Organization and Departmental Conflicts
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Arts. 269-305 — Departmental Autonomy
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's nine departments have significant autonomous powers under the 2009 constitution and Autonomy Law. Tensions persist between the progressive altiplano (La Paz, Oruro, Potosí) and the agribusiness-oriented Media Luna (Santa Cruz, Beni, Tarija, Pando). The 2008 Media Luna autonomy referendum — declared illegal by the national government — highlighted deep regional divisions that continue to shape Bolivian politics.
laws.penalty: Unconstitutional autonomy declarations: nullification; incitement to separatism: sedition charges
exceptions: Legitimate departmental autonomy referendums under OEP supervision recognized
Regional resource revenue sharing disputes resolved by Plurinational Constitutional Tribunal

quiz.q: What is the 'Media Luna' in Bolivian politics?
options: Four eastern lowland departments with agribusiness interests that sought greater autonomy
quiz.explanation: The 'Media Luna' (Half Moon) refers to Santa Cruz, Beni, Tarija, and Pando — Bolivia's eastern lowland departments that sought greater autonomy in 2008, reflecting deep economic and cultural differences with the altiplano.

laws.title: Mining Workers — FSTMB History
laws.subtitle: Labor Code and Mining Industry Worker Rights
laws.fullDescription: The Bolivian Mine Workers' Federation (FSTMB) has been one of Latin America's most historically militant unions. Mining workers at Siglo XX and Catavi mines participated in numerous uprisings, and were massacred at San Juan in 1967. The nationalized COMIBOL mines were eventually privatized under neoliberal reforms of the 1980s-90s, devastating the unionized workforce. Mining cooperatives partially replaced formal employment.
laws.penalty: Anti-union discrimination: fines and reinstatement; collective bargaining violations: mediation then sanctions
exceptions: Cooperative mine workers have different labor rights than employees
Essential service workers have restricted strike rights

quiz.q: What happened to Bolivia's COMIBOL state mines under 1980s neoliberal reforms?
options: Privatized, devastating the unionized mining workforce
quiz.explanation: The privatization and contraction of COMIBOL under DS 21060 (1985) devastated Bolivia's organized mine workers — eliminating tens of thousands of unionized jobs and dispersing workers to cooperative mining and urban informal sectors.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Rights — Civil Union Law
laws.subtitle: Law 807 — Gender Identity Law 2016
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Gender Identity Law 807 allows transgender individuals to change their legal name and gender on identity documents without requiring surgery or medical procedures. However, same-sex civil unions have been contentious — the Constitutional Tribunal ruled in 2023 that the constitution does not prohibit them, but full marriage equality has not been achieved. LGBTQ+ people face significant discrimination and violence.
laws.penalty: Discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity: fines; hate crimes: sentence enhancement
exceptions: Religious organizations may maintain internal doctrinal positions
Medical providers may conscientiously object to gender transition procedures

quiz.q: What did Bolivia's Gender Identity Law 807 allow without surgery?
options: Transgender individuals to change legal name and gender on documents
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Law 807 (2016) allows transgender individuals to change their name and gender marker on official documents without requiring surgery or medical certification — a progressive step, though marriage equality remains incomplete.

laws.title: Plurinational Economy — Mixed Economic Model
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Arts. 306-330 — Economic Model
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's constitution establishes a 'plural economy' combining state, private, cooperative, and community/indigenous economic forms. The state plays a strategic role through nationalized enterprises while private business operates alongside. Profit repatriation by foreign investors is permitted but regulated. The model achieved significant poverty reduction (from 60% to 35%) during the commodity boom years 2006-2014.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: 5–10 years plus full restitution; illicit capital flight: fines up to 100% of undeclared amount
exceptions: Reinvested profits taxed at reduced rate
Small community enterprises under simplified tax regime

quiz.q: By how much did Bolivia reduce its poverty rate during the commodity boom years?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia reduced its poverty rate from approximately 60% to 35% during the 2006-2014 commodity boom years — a major achievement attributed to hydrocarbon nationalization revenues funding social programs under the plural economy model.

laws.title: Anti-Drug Air Interdiction
laws.subtitle: Law 1008 and Air Sovereignty Decree
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia operates air interdiction to intercept drug trafficking flights, with authority to force down or shoot down aircraft suspected of carrying drugs. This power — also held by Colombia and Peru — is controversial internationally but has been upheld as an exercise of air sovereignty. The FELCN and military coordinate interdiction operations, with significant seizures of cocaine precursors and finished product annually.
laws.penalty: Drug air trafficking: 20–30 years; pilot of drug aircraft: additional 5 years for endangering aviation
exceptions: Emergency landings by distressed aircraft receive humanitarian consideration
Government aircraft have full air freedom

quiz.q: What controversial power does Bolivia's anti-drug law grant regarding suspected drug trafficking aircraft?
options: Authority to force down or shoot down suspected drug planes
Interception but only over national territory
quiz.explanation: Bolivia, like Colombia and Peru, asserts air sovereignty rights to force down or shoot down suspected drug trafficking aircraft — a controversial but widely practiced power justified as necessary for aerial drug interdiction.

laws.title: Carnival and Cultural Heritage
laws.subtitle: Oruro Carnival UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Oruro Carnival — one of UNESCO's masterpieces of oral and intangible cultural heritage — blends indigenous Andean rituals with Catholic influence. The Diablada dance and other dances feature prominently. Bolivia has enacted cultural protection laws for the carnival and similar events. Disputes with Peru and Chile over cultural heritage claims (like the tinku and other traditions) reflect Andean cultural politics.
laws.penalty: Commercial exploitation of Oruro Carnival imagery without authorization: intellectual property violation; counterfeiting costumes: fines
exceptions: Non-commercial cultural celebrations of shared Andean heritage recognized
Academic research and documentation freely permitted

quiz.q: What UNESCO designation does Bolivia's Oruro Carnival hold?
options: Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Cultural Heritage
quiz.explanation: Oruro Carnival has been UNESCO-recognized as a Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Cultural Heritage — its Diablada and other dances blending pre-Columbian Andean spirituality with Catholic syncretism in spectacular fashion.

laws.title: Salar de Uyuni Protection
laws.subtitle: Environmental Protection and Lithium Law Intersection
laws.fullDescription: The Salar de Uyuni is the world's largest salt flat (10,582 km²) and also contains the world's largest lithium reserves. Bolivia has balanced environmental protection of this unique ecosystem with industrialization plans. The salar supports flamingo breeding and other endemic species. Environmental impact assessments are required for all industrial activities, though the scale of planned lithium operations raises concerns about hydrology and biodiversity.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized extraction from Salar: criminal prosecution; environmental damage: fines per hectare
exceptions: Scientific research with SERNAP permits
YLB authorized operations under environmental management plan

quiz.q: What dual significance does Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni have?
options: World's largest salt flat AND location of world's largest lithium reserves
quiz.explanation: The Salar de Uyuni is simultaneously the world's largest salt flat (stunning tourist destination and unique ecosystem) and the world's largest lithium reserve — creating a challenging tension between environmental protection and industrial development.

laws.title: Deforestation and Land Title Fraud
laws.subtitle: INRA Law and Forest Crime
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's land reform and titling process has been marred by fraud, with illegal deforestation often preceding fraudulent land title applications. The National Land Reform Institute (INRA) has faced corruption allegations in its titling processes. Forest crimes — burning and clearing to claim agricultural land — are common. Bolivia's deforestation rate has been among the highest in South America, driven partly by fraudulent land grabs.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent land titling: 5–10 years; deforestation for fraud: 5–12 years; INRA official corruption: 8–15 years
exceptions: Legitimate agrarian reform beneficiaries under Law 1715 protected
Small-scale subsistence clearing under simplified procedure

quiz.q: How does illegal deforestation relate to land fraud in Bolivia?
options: Burning and clearing land is used to establish occupation before fraudulent land title applications
Land fraud only involves urban property
quiz.explanation: A common land fraud pattern in Bolivia involves illegally burning and clearing forest to establish physical occupation of land — then filing fraudulent title applications claiming it as productive land, contributing to Bolivia's high deforestation rate.

laws.title: Potosí Silver Mountain — Cerro Rico
laws.subtitle: Mining Patrimony and Structural Instability Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Cerro Rico de Potosí — the mountain that funded the Spanish Empire for centuries through silver extraction — remains a working mine employing thousands of cooperative miners. The mountain faces catastrophic structural collapse due to centuries of tunneling. UNESCO and geologists have warned of collapse risk. Bolivia's laws govern mining rights, worker safety, and preservation of the UNESCO World Heritage city below. The tension between heritage and continued mining is unresolved.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized mining outside designated zones: criminal prosecution; safety violations causing death: 15–20 years
exceptions: Traditional cooperative mining in designated zones continues under Law 535
Emergency evacuation protocols override normal mining licenses

quiz.q: What danger does Cerro Rico in Potosí face from centuries of mining?
options: Structural collapse due to extensive tunneling — threatening the UNESCO city below
quiz.explanation: Cerro Rico has been so extensively tunneled for silver over 500 years that geologists warn of potential catastrophic collapse — threatening both thousands of working miners and the UNESCO World Heritage colonial city of Potosí below.

laws.title: Digital Bolivia — E-Government Strategy
laws.subtitle: DS 1793 — Digital Government Decree
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's e-government strategy established online services for birth registration, tax filing, and government procedures. The ADSIB (Agency for Information Society Development) coordinates digital infrastructure. Bolivia has made progress in mobile banking (particularly SINTESIS system) for social benefit payments. Internet penetration has grown significantly, though rural areas lag. Bolivia's TUPAC KATARI satellite supports rural connectivity.
laws.penalty: Cybercrime against government systems: 5–15 years; data breaches of citizen information: fines
exceptions: Government websites must be accessible regardless of disability
Emergency digital procedures available during natural disasters

quiz.q: What satellite did Bolivia launch to support rural digital connectivity?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's TUPAC KATARI satellite (launched 2013) was named after a major indigenous hero — a symbolic assertion of technological sovereignty, providing satellite internet and telecommunications to underserved rural communities.

laws.title: Judicial Elections — Organic Law of the Judiciary
laws.subtitle: Law 025 — Judicial Organ 2010
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia popularly elects Supreme Court, Agro-Environmental Court, and Constitutional Tribunal judges — an experiment in judicial democracy unique globally. Candidates must be pre-approved by the Plurinational Assembly (politically dominated), then elected by popular vote. Critics argue this politicizes courts; defenders say it democratizes an elite institution. Judicial performance has been widely criticized, with extreme case backlogs.
laws.penalty: Judicial corruption: criminal prosecution plus removal; case manipulation: 5–10 years; perversion of justice: 8–15 years
exceptions: Lower court judges still appointed through civil service competition
Judicial discipline handled by Council of the Magistracy (Consejo de la Magistratura)

quiz.q: What is unique about how Bolivia selects its Supreme Court judges?
options: Popular election by all citizens — unique in the world
quiz.explanation: Bolivia holds popular elections for Supreme Court, Constitutional Tribunal, and other high court judges — the only country in the world to do so. While democratically innovative, critics argue it politicizes justice through Assembly candidate pre-screening.

laws.title: Money Laundering — UIAF
laws.subtitle: Law 170 — Anti-Money Laundering 2011
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Anti-Money Laundering Law created the Financial Intelligence Unit (UIAF), required banks to report suspicious transactions, and criminalized money laundering. The law was strengthened after Bolivia was placed on FATF's grey list. Drug trafficking proceeds represent the primary money laundering threat, along with corruption from natural resource revenues. Real estate, informal gold trading, and the financial system are key laundering vectors.
laws.penalty: Money laundering: 8–15 years; failure to report suspicious transactions: fines up to BOB 500,000
exceptions: Notaries and lawyers subject to professional reporting obligations with legal privilege limitations
Cash-based businesses in informal economy have reporting thresholds adjusted

quiz.q: Why was Bolivia's anti-money laundering law strengthened significantly?
options: FATF grey-listing requiring action to improve the AML/CFT framework
quiz.explanation: Bolivia was grey-listed by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), requiring it to strengthen anti-money laundering laws — a key driver of Law 170 and UIAF creation, necessary to avoid financial isolation.

laws.title: Bolivian Navy — Landlocked Maritime Service
laws.subtitle: Law 1074 — Navy Day and Maritime Aspiration
laws.fullDescription: Despite having no sea access since 1884, Bolivia maintains a navy — the 'Bolivian Navy' or Armada Boliviana — which operates on Lake Titicaca and major Amazonian rivers. The navy symbolizes Bolivia's maritime aspiration and maintains river patrol and border functions. Every March 23, Bolivia observes 'Day of the Sea' (Día del Mar) to commemorate its lost Pacific coast, and the navy marches through La Paz.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized vessel operation on Lake Titicaca or Bolivian rivers: seizure and fines
exceptions: Foreign fishing vessels with bilateral agreements have limited access to shared border waters
Tourist vessels on Lake Titicaca under SERNAPESC oversight

quiz.q: Why does Bolivia maintain a navy despite having no ocean coast?
options: It operates on Lake Titicaca and Amazon rivers, symbolizing maritime aspiration and border patrol
It was mandated by a UN treaty
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's navy operates on Lake Titicaca and Amazon tributaries for border patrol and river transport — while also serving as a powerful symbol of Bolivia's aspiration to regain its Pacific coast lost in the 1884 War of the Pacific.

laws.title: Madidi National Park Biodiversity
laws.subtitle: SERNAP Management and Ecotourism Law
