laws.fullDescription: Madidi National Park in northern Bolivia is among the world's most biodiverse protected areas, containing extraordinary numbers of bird, mammal, and plant species. Bolivia's SERNAP (National Protected Area Service) manages it under a buffer zone model that allows indigenous communities to conduct ecotourism. The Chalalan Ecolodge — community-owned and pioneer ecotourism model — has been internationally recognized.
laws.penalty: Poaching in Madidi: 5–15 years; illegal logging: 5–10 years; unauthorized tourism operations: license revocation
exceptions: Indigenous communities in Madidi buffer zones have ancestral use rights
Scientific research with SERNAP authorization

quiz.q: What is Madidi National Park globally recognized for?
options: Being among the world's most biodiverse protected areas
quiz.explanation: Madidi National Park is among the world's most biodiverse protected areas — its extraordinary species density across altitudinal gradients from Amazon lowlands to Andean peaks makes it a crown jewel of Bolivia's protected area system.

laws.title: Plurinational State — Decolonization
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Arts. 1-10 and Decolonization Vice Ministry
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's identity as a 'Plurinational State' (Estado Plurinacional) represents a fundamental break from the colonial republic model. The state formally rejects colonialism, recognizes indigenous civilizations as foundational, and uses Wiphala (indigenous flag) alongside the national flag. The Vice Ministry of Decolonization runs programs to challenge structural racism in institutions. Indigenous languages are co-official alongside Spanish.
laws.penalty: Institutional discrimination based on indigenous identity: administrative sanctions; hate speech targeting indigenous peoples: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Cultural practices must respect individual rights — internal community rules cannot override constitutional rights
Decolonization programs are education-focused, not punitive for past colonial acts

quiz.q: How many languages does Bolivia's constitution recognize as official?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's 2009 constitution declares Spanish and 36 indigenous languages as co-official — including Quechua, Aymara, Guaraní, and 33 others — the most indigenous language recognitions of any national constitution in the world.

laws.title: Witness Protection Program
laws.subtitle: Law 458 — Witness and Victim Protection 2013
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Witness Protection Law created a formal program to protect witnesses and victims in serious criminal cases, particularly drug trafficking, organized crime, and corruption. The program offers identity changes, relocation, and financial support. Implementation has been hampered by limited resources and institutional distrust, with witnesses in high-profile cases sometimes declining to testify despite legal protections.
laws.penalty: Witness intimidation: 5–10 years; retaliation against protected witness: 10–15 years
exceptions: Anonymous testimony permitted in trafficking and organized crime cases
Victims may testify via video link from secure location

quiz.q: What services does Bolivia's witness protection program offer?
options: Identity changes, relocation, and financial support
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Law 458 witness protection program offers identity changes, relocation to new locations, and financial support — though limited resources mean the program struggles to fully protect witnesses in dangerous cases.

laws.title: Organic Agriculture and Agroecology
laws.subtitle: Law 3525 — Organic Agricultural Production Regulation 2006
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's agroecology law promotes organic and sustainable agriculture, particularly in the highlands where traditional practices align with organic principles. The law established certification systems for organic products and created incentives for small farmers. Bolivia exports organic quinoa, cacao, and Brazil nuts — products where traditional farming methods produce premium products for international markets.
laws.penalty: False organic certification: fines and certification revocation; fraud in organic exports: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Traditional subsistence farming need not be certified but can claim traditional production status
Transition period of 3 years for farms converting to organic

quiz.q: Name a major Bolivian organic export product.
options: Quinoa (along with cacao and Brazil nuts)
quiz.explanation: Bolivia is a major exporter of organic quinoa — a grain native to the Andes grown for centuries by indigenous communities — along with organic cacao and Brazil nuts, earning premium prices on international markets.

laws.title: Juana Azurduy Maternal Health Bonus
laws.subtitle: DS 066 — Juana Azurduy Bonus 2009
laws.fullDescription: The Juana Azurduy conditional cash transfer provides payments to pregnant women and mothers who attend prenatal checkups, give birth in health facilities, and bring children for growth monitoring up to age 2. Named after an independence heroine, it targets Bolivia's high maternal mortality rate — among South America's highest. The program has been credited with increasing facility births and prenatal care utilization.
laws.penalty: False claims of checkup attendance: restitution plus 50% penalty; health worker fraud: dismissal and prosecution
exceptions: Women in remote areas without health facilities may access mobile health teams
Emergency deliveries outside facilities still qualify

quiz.q: What behaviors does Bolivia's Juana Azurduy bonus incentivize?
options: Prenatal checkups, facility births, and child growth monitoring
quiz.explanation: The Juana Azurduy bonus is a conditional cash transfer paid to mothers who attend prenatal checkups, deliver in health facilities, and bring children for growth monitoring — targeting Bolivia's high maternal and infant mortality rates.

laws.title: Social Control and Citizen Participation
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Arts. 241-242 — Social Control
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's constitution creates a unique 'social control' mechanism allowing civil society organizations to oversee and audit state institutions. Social control bodies can request information, denounce irregularities, and participate in policy formulation. In practice, the mechanism has been used by pro-government organizations to validate government actions, while independent civil society monitoring has faced obstacles.
laws.penalty: Obstruction of social control bodies: administrative sanctions; disclosure of control findings in bad faith: potential liability
exceptions: State security information exempt from social control scrutiny
Commercial confidentiality in public contracts may limit disclosure

quiz.q: What unique oversight mechanism does Bolivia's constitution create?
options: Social control — allowing civil society to audit and oversee state institutions
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's constitution (Arts. 241-242) creates 'social control' — a formal role for organized civil society to monitor government institutions, request information, and participate in policy. Critics note it has sometimes been captured by pro-government groups.

laws.title: Public Investment and Infrastructure
laws.subtitle: SNIP — National Public Investment System
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's National Public Investment System (SNIP) coordinates public investment across central government, departments, and municipalities. Infrastructure investment surged under Morales — roads, schools, hospitals, sports facilities, and the La Paz cable car. Critics noted some projects prioritized political visibility over economic returns. International financing from China, Brazil, CAF, and IDB funded major infrastructure.
laws.penalty: Corruption in public contracting: Law 004 applies; 5–15 years plus restitution
exceptions: Emergency infrastructure procurement uses simplified procedures
Community small projects under BOB 1 million use direct award

quiz.q: Which multilateral lender has been a major infrastructure financier for Bolivia alongside China?
quiz.explanation: CAF (Development Bank of Latin America) and the IDB (Inter-American Development Bank) have been major financiers of Bolivian infrastructure, alongside Chinese loans — funding roads, energy, and social infrastructure.

laws.title: Cybercrime Law
laws.subtitle: Law 164 Chapter V — ICT Crimes
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's telecommunications law includes provisions against cybercrime, including unauthorized system access, digital fraud, and harmful content distribution. The law is considered inadequate by cybersecurity experts — Bolivia has one of the region's weakest cyber legal frameworks. Government systems have been targets of attacks, and the financial sector has experienced significant cyber fraud. A standalone cybercrime law has been proposed but not enacted.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized computer access: 1–4 years; cyber fraud: 3–8 years; distributing malware: 2–6 years
exceptions: Authorized penetration testing by certified professionals exempt
Security researchers under responsible disclosure programs

quiz.q: How is Bolivia's cybercrime legal framework evaluated by experts?
options: Among the strongest in Latin America
Inadequate — one of the region's weakest cyber legal frameworks
quiz.explanation: Cybersecurity experts consider Bolivia's cyber legal framework — primarily embedded in the Telecommunications Law rather than standalone legislation — one of Latin America's weakest, leaving significant gaps in addressing cyber threats.

laws.title: Defensoría del Pueblo — Ombudsman
laws.subtitle: Law 870 — Defensoría del Pueblo 2016
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Defensoría del Pueblo (People's Defender) is an independent constitutional institution that receives complaints against government institutions, investigates human rights violations, and issues recommendations. It has played important roles in documenting political violence, indigenous rights violations, and prison conditions. The Defensoría's independence has been questioned when its leadership has had perceived political alignments.
laws.penalty: Obstruction of Defensoría investigations: contempt charges; failure to respond to Defensoría recommendations: administrative sanction
exceptions: Military and intelligence operations have limited disclosure obligations
Diplomatic missions exempt from Defensoría jurisdiction

quiz.q: What is the role of Bolivia's Defensoría del Pueblo?
options: An independent ombudsman investigating human rights complaints against government
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Defensoría del Pueblo is an independent ombudsman that investigates human rights violations, receives complaints against government institutions, and issues recommendations — playing a key role in political violence documentation.

laws.title: Sunflower and Soy Export Regulation
laws.subtitle: Agricultural Export Policy and Santa Cruz Production
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Santa Cruz lowlands produce significant quantities of soybeans and sunflower for export, primarily to Colombia, Peru, and Andean Community countries. The Andean Community allows Bolivia to export agricultural products preferentially. Export quotas and restrictions fluctuate based on domestic food security needs — restricting exports during food price spikes and encouraging them when foreign exchange is needed.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized exports during restriction periods: 100% fine on export value; falsification of phytosanitary certificates: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Organic certified products under premium export regime
MERCOSUR associate member preferences for certain agricultural products

quiz.q: To which trade bloc does Bolivia preferentially export soybeans and sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia exports soybeans and sunflower to Andean Community countries (Colombia, Peru, Ecuador) under preferential tariff arrangements — with Santa Cruz's agribusiness sector forming a major part of Bolivia's export base.

laws.title: Prefectures to Governorates — Decentralization
laws.subtitle: Autonomy Law and Departmental Government Reform
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia replaced its appointed departmental prefects with elected governors under the 2009 constitution and Autonomy Law — a major democratic decentralization. Governors lead departmental governments with autonomous budgets and competencies. The Santa Cruz governor has been a particularly powerful political figure, sometimes positioning as opposition leader to the national government. The 2021 arrest of Santa Cruz Governor Luis Fernando Camacho added to political tensions.
laws.penalty: Governors exceeding autonomous competencies: Constitutional Tribunal review; corruption: Law 004 applies
exceptions: National security matters remain exclusively national
Emergency declarations may temporarily override departmental autonomy

quiz.q: What replaced Bolivia's appointed departmental prefects?
options: Elected governors with autonomous budgets under the 2009 constitution
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's 2009 constitution replaced appointed departmental prefects with democratically elected governors — a major decentralization creating powerful regional leaders, like Santa Cruz's governor who has become a leading opposition figure.

laws.title: Zero Malnutrition Program
laws.subtitle: CONAN and Multi-Sector Nutrition Strategy
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia has combated childhood malnutrition through the Zero Malnutrition Program (PAN 0 Malnutrición), combining supplementary feeding, micronutrient supplementation, and community health workers. Bolivia has made significant progress reducing chronic malnutrition, particularly in indigenous highland communities where stunting rates were very high. The program is funded by hydrocarbons revenues and international cooperation.
laws.penalty: Fraud in food aid distribution: criminal prosecution; diversion of nutrition supplements: 3–8 years
exceptions: Emergency nutritional interventions during natural disasters bypass normal procurement
Traditional complementary foods recognized alongside commercial supplements

quiz.q: What funded Bolivia's Zero Malnutrition program?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Zero Malnutrition program is funded by a combination of hydrocarbon revenues (from the nationalized oil and gas sector) and international cooperation — demonstrating how resource nationalization directly finances social programs.

laws.title: Police Reform and DIPAM
laws.subtitle: Organic Police Law and Anti-Corruption in Police
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's National Police has faced chronic corruption allegations, particularly regarding drug trafficking complicity and human rights abuses. The Internal Affairs Directorate (DIPAM) investigates police misconduct. Under Morales, police were partially displaced by loyal social movements for security functions. The 2019 crisis involved police mutinies. Major reforms have been promised but not systematically implemented.
laws.penalty: Police corruption: dismissal plus 5–15 years; extortion: 3–8 years; police killing in excess of force: 15–25 years
exceptions: Undercover operations authorized by prosecutor have immunity for infiltration activities
Excessive force in genuine self-defense subject to proportionality review

quiz.q: What entity investigates police misconduct in Bolivia?
quiz.explanation: DIPAM (Dirección de Investigación de Procedimientos Administrativos y Moralización) is Bolivia's internal affairs unit investigating police misconduct — though critics say it lacks genuine independence from the institution it monitors.

laws.title: Wildlife Trafficking
laws.subtitle: Law 1333 and Penal Code Environmental Crimes
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia is a biodiversity hotspot and source country for wildlife trafficking, including jaguars (for Chinese market), parrots, and medicinal animals. The Environmental Law 1333 and Penal Code provisions criminalize wildlife trafficking with escalating penalties. Bolivia participates in CITES. Jaguar trafficking surged as Chinese demand for jaguar parts grew, linked to infrastructure workers from Chinese construction projects.
laws.penalty: Wildlife trafficking: 5–15 years; jaguar trafficking: up to 15 years; organized wildlife crime: 10–20 years
exceptions: Licensed zoos and research institutions may hold protected species
Indigenous communities may use wildlife for traditional purposes with SERNAP oversight

quiz.q: What unexpected link has been identified in Bolivia's jaguar trafficking crisis?
options: Chinese infrastructure workers creating demand for jaguar parts for the Chinese market
quiz.explanation: Jaguar trafficking in Bolivia surged partly due to demand from Chinese workers on construction projects, who created a market for jaguar teeth, skins, and parts destined for China — a concerning nexus of infrastructure and wildlife crime.

laws.title: Disability Pension — SENADIS
laws.subtitle: Law 223 Arts. 63-70 — Disability Cash Transfer
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia provides disability pensions and subsidies through SENADIS (National Service for Persons with Disabilities). Persons with severe disabilities receive monthly cash transfers and free healthcare. The 'Awareness Month' and the famous long marches by disabled protesters brought national attention to underfunded programs. Bolivia ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and incorporated its principles into Law 223.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent disability pension claims: restitution plus criminal prosecution; discrimination by employers: fines and injunctions
exceptions: Disability assessment carried out by interdisciplinary teams — appeals process available
Temporary disabilities have separate short-term benefit provisions

quiz.q: What famous form of protest have Bolivian persons with disabilities used to demand better support?
options: Long marches from Cochabamba to La Paz — sometimes hundreds of kilometers
quiz.explanation: Bolivian persons with disabilities repeatedly organized grueling cross-country marches — sometimes hundreds of kilometers from Cochabamba to La Paz — to demand improved benefits, generating national media attention and policy responses.

laws.title: Right to Revolution — Social Resistance
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Art. 25 and Historical Social Movements
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's constitution recognizes the right of the people to resist oppression and tyranny — a provision reflecting Bolivia's history of popular uprisings. The Water War (2000), Gas War (2003), and 2019 crisis all involved mass mobilization that changed governments. Bolivia's labor confederation COB and indigenous movements CONAMAQ and CIDOB are constitutional actors recognized as legitimate social forces.
laws.penalty: Armed rebellion against constitutional government: treason (20–30 years); peaceful resistance is constitutionally protected
exceptions: Constitutional protection applies to peaceful resistance — violent uprising treated as sedition
Social movements cannot override constitutional rights of individuals

quiz.q: What major popular uprising in 2003 changed Bolivian government policy on gas exports?
options: The Gas War of 2003 — forcing President Sánchez de Lozada to resign
quiz.explanation: The Gas War of 2003 — mass protests against plans to export Bolivian natural gas through Chile — forced President Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada to resign and flee, directly leading to Evo Morales's eventual rise to the presidency.

laws.title: Femicide Investigation Protocol
laws.subtitle: Law 348 Art. 84 and Prosecution Protocol
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia developed specialized femicide investigation protocols under Law 348, requiring forensic analysis, rapid response teams, and specialized prosecutors. The FELCV (Special Force Against Violence) handles gender violence cases. Despite these mechanisms, Bolivia's femicide rate remains among Latin America's highest and conviction rates are low. Prosecutors report insufficient forensic resources and witness cooperation challenges.
laws.penalty: Femicide: 30 years without parole; attempted femicide: 15–20 years; failure of officials to process femicide report: disciplinary action
exceptions: Psychological incapacity at time of crime subject to psychiatric evaluation and possible reduced culpability
Self-defense in response to imminent domestic violence is a complete defense

quiz.q: What specialized police force handles gender violence cases in Bolivia?
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's FELCV (Fuerza Especial de Lucha Contra la Violencia) is the specialized police unit handling gender violence and femicide cases — though chronic underfunding and resource constraints limit its effectiveness despite Law 348's strong provisions.

laws.title: Monetary Policy and BCB Independence
laws.subtitle: Law 1670 — Central Bank of Bolivia
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Central Bank (BCB) operates under Law 1670 with a mandate of monetary stability. Under the Morales era, the BCB effectively financed state enterprises and social programs — departing from orthodox independence. The bolivianization policy succeeded in reducing dollarization. The 2023-24 foreign reserve crisis strained BCB credibility as it ran low on dollar reserves needed for currency defense and fuel imports.
laws.penalty: Counterfeiting boliviano currency: 10–15 years; unauthorized foreign exchange operations: fines up to BOB 200,000
exceptions: BCB emergency instruments available during financial crises
Foreign currency accounts for international trade purposes permitted

quiz.q: What unorthodox role did Bolivia's BCB play under the Morales economic model?
options: Financing state enterprises and social programs — departing from orthodox central bank independence
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's BCB under Morales departed from orthodox central bank independence by financing state enterprises (YPFB, ENDE, etc.) and social programs — a heterodox approach that supported Bolivia's growth model but contributed to later reserve depletion.

laws.title: Women's Political Participation
laws.subtitle: Electoral Law Parity and 'Chachawarmi' Principle
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia has achieved one of the world's highest rates of women in parliament — consistently above 50% in the Plurinational Assembly — through strict gender parity and alternation requirements in electoral law. The Aymara concept of 'chachawarmi' (complementary male-female pair governance) influenced constitutional provisions. Bolivia has elected female mayors, governors, and ministers in large numbers.
laws.penalty: Electoral lists without gender parity: rejected by OEP; harassment of women politicians (political violence against women): 2–5 years under Law 243
exceptions: Indigenous community selections using traditional methods may deviate from parity if culturally justified
Vacancies filled maintaining original gender of outgoing member

quiz.q: What proportion of Bolivia's Plurinational Assembly are women?
options: Over 50% — one of the world's highest
quiz.explanation: Bolivia consistently achieves over 50% women in its Plurinational Assembly — among the world's highest rates — due to strict gender parity and alternation rules in electoral law, alongside the indigenous 'chachawarmi' complementarity principle.

laws.title: Prison Crisis and SNAI Reform
laws.subtitle: Law 2298 — Prison Execution Regime
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's prisons suffer extreme overcrowding — capacity for roughly 5,000 prisoners holds over 22,000. The San Pedro prison in La Paz became infamous for internal self-governance, drug markets, and even tourist visits. Multiple prison riots and fires have killed prisoners. Prison reform efforts under SENADEP and Law 2298 have had limited impact. FELCV and judicial reforms aim to reduce the pretrial detention driving overcrowding.
laws.penalty: Prison riots — instigators: 5–10 years additional; prison escape: 1–3 years additional; aiding escape: 2–5 years
exceptions: Humanitarian release for terminally ill prisoners available
Alternative sentencing for non-violent offenders reduces overcrowding

quiz.q: What became internationally famous about La Paz's San Pedro prison?
options: Its internal self-governance, drug markets, and even tourist visits
quiz.explanation: San Pedro prison in La Paz became internationally famous — and the subject of a memoir (Marching Powder) — for its unique internal economy, self-governance, resident families, and drug market, even attracting backpacker tourists seeking guided tours.

laws.title: Climate Change National Policy
laws.subtitle: Law 300 Framework of Mother Earth and Climate Change
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Framework Law 300 (2012) for Mother Earth and Integral Development for Living Well established climate change adaptation as a national priority. Bolivia is highly vulnerable to climate change — glacial retreat threatens water security, El Niño cycles intensify droughts and floods, and Amazon deforestation accelerates warming. Bolivia has simultaneously criticized developed countries for climate debt while facing criticism for its own deforestation.
laws.penalty: Climate-negligent industrial practices: fines and mandatory mitigation; carbon market fraud: criminal prosecution
exceptions: National Development Plan projects granted transition periods for emissions reduction
Traditional slash-and-burn farming under 1 hectare has tolerance provisions

quiz.q: What concept links Bolivia's climate policy to its Mother Earth law?
options: Living Well (Vivir Bien) — integral development in harmony with nature
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's climate policy is framed around 'Vivir Bien' (Living Well) — the Andean concept of harmonious development embedded in Law 300 and the constitution — positioning climate action as part of decolonizing development rather than just technical mitigation.

laws.title: Right to Education — Public University Access
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Art. 17 and University Free Access
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's constitution guarantees the right to free education at all levels including university. Public universities are free and constitutionally autonomous. The entrance exam system limits access at some universities, while others have open enrollment. Literacy campaigns under Morales, supported by Cuban advisors using the 'Yo Sí Puedo' method, were declared to have eliminated illiteracy by 2008 — though contested by some analysts.
laws.penalty: Denial of school access based on inability to pay fees: administrative sanction; discrimination in admissions: fines
exceptions: Private universities may charge tuition for additional programs
Technical and vocational institutions may charge nominal registration fees

quiz.q: What Cuban method was used in Bolivia's literacy campaign?
options: Yo Sí Puedo — used by Cuban advisors, declared to eliminate illiteracy by 2008
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's literacy campaign used Cuba's 'Yo Sí Puedo' (Yes I Can) audiovisual method, with Cuban advisors supporting the effort. Bolivia declared itself free of illiteracy in 2008 — though independent analysts questioned the completeness of the achievement.

laws.title: BoA — Boliviana de Aviación
laws.subtitle: National Airline Re-Nationalization
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia re-nationalized its airline, creating Boliviana de Aviación (BoA) in 2009 after the collapse of Lloyd Aéreo Boliviano. BoA operates domestic and international routes. The airline has expanded connections to Brazil, Argentina, Spain, and the US. State airlines in Latin America have mixed records — BoA has been subsidized but provides strategic connectivity for a landlocked country with challenging mountain terrain.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized air operations without DGAC license: criminal prosecution; aviation safety violations: license suspension
exceptions: Emergency humanitarian flights may operate under simplified authorization
Military aviation exempt from commercial regulations

quiz.q: Why is air connectivity particularly strategic for Bolivia?
options: Bolivia is landlocked with challenging mountain terrain — air is critical for domestic and international connection
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's landlocked status and extreme Andean terrain make air transport critically important — BoA's state airline ensures domestic connectivity across mountainous regions where ground travel is slow, and international connections to Brazil, Argentina, and Europe.

laws.title: Corruption Investigation — CIRC
laws.subtitle: Law 004 and Specialized Anti-Corruption Courts
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia created specialized anti-corruption courts and prosecutors under Law 004, with the CIRC (Integrated Register of Corruption Cases) tracking major cases. High-profile corruption cases have involved contracts in the energy sector, public works, and social programs. The 'Zapatazo' scandal involved irregularities in the Air Force. Political polarization has made it difficult to distinguish legitimate prosecution from politically motivated cases.
laws.penalty: Embezzlement of public funds: 5–15 years plus restitution of 3× amount; corruption in public contracts: 8–20 years
exceptions: Voluntary disclosure before investigation reduces penalty
Cooperation agreements with prosecutors may reduce sentences by up to one-third

quiz.q: What does Bolivia's CIRC track?
options: Integrated Register of Corruption Cases across all investigations
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's CIRC (Registro Integrado de Casos de Corrupción) tracks and coordinates major corruption investigations — a tool of Law 004's expanded anti-corruption framework, though political polarization makes distinguishing legitimate from politicized cases difficult.

laws.title: TIPNIS and Indigenous Territory Rights
laws.subtitle: Law 180 and 222 — TIPNIS Protection
laws.fullDescription: The TIPNIS territory (4.5 million hectares) is simultaneously a national park and indigenous territory for Mojeño, Yuracaré, and Chimán peoples. Law 180 (2011) declared it intangible after mass indigenous marches. Law 222 (2012) enabled a consultation process that indigenous groups rejected as imposed. The territory remains contested between conservation, indigenous sovereignty, and Chapare coca farmers seeking expansion.
laws.penalty: Illegal settlement in TIPNIS intangible zone: forced removal; resource extraction: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Indigenous inhabitants have ancestral use rights within their territory
Scientific research with indigenous community consent and SERNAP permit

quiz.q: What triggered Law 180 declaring TIPNIS territory intangible?
options: Mass indigenous marches — the VIII and IX Marches — opposing a planned highway through the territory
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's historic VIII and IX Indigenous Marches — thousands of indigenous people walking hundreds of kilometers from the Amazon to La Paz — forced the government to pass Law 180 declaring TIPNIS intangible, though subsequent Law 222 reversed course.

laws.title: Energy Transition and Renewables
laws.subtitle: ENDE Renewables and Law 835 Energy Policy
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia has significant renewable energy potential — hydroelectric, solar (highest solar irradiance in the world in the altiplano), wind (Uyuni area), and geothermal. ENDE is developing solar plants and Bolivia aims to become a regional energy exporter. The energy matrix has historically depended on natural gas. The 2023-24 energy crisis — caused partly by underinvestment and declining gas output — accelerated renewable energy planning.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized energy generation: AETN fines; theft from national grid: 3–8 years
exceptions: Community off-grid solar and micro-hydro under rural electrification program simplified approval
Residential solar systems below 10kW under net metering without license

quiz.q: What solar resource advantage does Bolivia's altiplano have?
options: Among the world's highest solar irradiance — making it ideal for solar energy
The sun is blocked by cloud cover
Solar only works in the Amazon
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's altiplano has among the world's highest solar irradiance due to its high altitude, dry climate, and proximity to the equator — giving Bolivia enormous solar energy potential, particularly around the Salar de Uyuni area.

laws.title: Coca as Cultural Heritage
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Art. 384 — Coca Protection
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's 2009 constitution uniquely declares coca a cultural heritage of the Bolivian people, mandating its protection, promotion, and commercialization in its natural state. This constitutional protection was the legal basis for Bolivia's withdrawal from and re-entry to the UN Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs. The constitution forbids the criminalization of coca leaf — distinct from coca paste or cocaine — creating a unique constitutional protection.
laws.penalty: Destruction of legally cultivated coca: compensation liability; criminalization of traditional coca use: unconstitutional
exceptions: Cocaine and coca paste remain illegal — the protection applies only to the natural coca leaf
Excess cultivation beyond Law 906 quotas may be eradicated

quiz.q: What does Bolivia's 2009 constitution declare about the coca leaf?
options: That it is a dangerous drug
That it is cultural heritage of the Bolivian people, mandating its protection
That it can be freely exported as cocaine
quiz.explanation: Article 384 of Bolivia's constitution declares coca 'ancestral cultural patrimony' of the Bolivian people and mandates its protection, promotion, and commercialization in natural form — a unique constitutional protection creating tension with international drug conventions.

laws.title: Environmental Defenders Protection
laws.subtitle: Aarhus Principles and Bolivian Environmental Law
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia has seen killings and threats against environmental defenders, particularly those opposing mining, deforestation, and hydrocarbon projects in indigenous territories. The constitution and Law 071 provide theoretical protection for environmental defenders, but practical protection has been inadequate. International bodies including the UN Special Rapporteur have raised concerns about criminalization of indigenous environmental activists.
laws.penalty: Killing of environmental defender: aggravated homicide charge; threats and harassment: 3–8 years; criminalization for legal advocacy: constitutional violation
exceptions: Advocates working through recognized indigenous consultation processes have procedural protections
International organizations supporting environmental defenders have legal standing

quiz.q: What international monitoring has occurred regarding Bolivian environmental defenders?
options: UN Special Rapporteur raised concerns about criminalization of indigenous environmental activists
quiz.explanation: The UN Special Rapporteur on Environmental Defenders has raised concerns about Bolivia criminalizing indigenous activists opposing mining and deforestation projects — a pattern observed across Latin America where resource extraction interests conflict with indigenous land rights.

laws.title: Narco-State Allegations and Drug Policy
laws.subtitle: UNODC Monitoring and Bolivia-US Relations
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia has faced allegations of narco-state tendencies under both Morales and subsequent governments — with coca federation leaders, police, and officials accused of drug trafficking complicity. The expulsion of DEA reduced international counter-narcotics cooperation. UNODC monitoring shows coca cultivation expanding. Bolivia has invested in alternative development and coca industrialization as alternatives to eradication, with mixed effectiveness against cocaine production.
laws.penalty: Narco-corruption by officials: 15–25 years; protecting trafficking organizations: 10–20 years; money laundering with narco proceeds: 10–15 years
exceptions: Witnesses in narco-state investigations receive protection under Law 458
International cooperation for extradition requires bilateral treaty

quiz.q: How did Bolivia change its counter-narcotics strategy after expelling the DEA?
options: Invested in alternative development and coca industrialization rather than eradication
Joined a new international drug agency
quiz.explanation: After expelling the DEA, Bolivia shifted to a 'social control' approach — working with coca union federations to limit cultivation while investing in alternative livelihoods and coca industrialization, rather than forced eradication backed by US agents.

laws.title: Amazon River Rights
laws.subtitle: Bolivia's Amazon Basin Policy and ACTO
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's Amazon tributaries — including the Madeira, Beni, Mamoré, and Iténez rivers — connect to the broader Amazon system. Constitutional provisions protecting water and the Amazon ecosystem, combined with Law 071 Mother Earth rights, provide a framework for river protection. Bolivia participates in ACTO and has bilateral agreements with Brazil on the Madeira River including shared management of hydroelectric impacts.
laws.penalty: Pollution of Amazon tributaries: criminal prosecution; illegal gold mining with mercury use: 8–15 years
exceptions: Traditional indigenous river navigation rights protected
Authorized hydroelectric research with environmental monitoring

quiz.q: What provides constitutional protection for Bolivia's Amazon rivers?
options: The Mother Earth Law 071 granting legal rights to nature, including water systems
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's Law 071 (Rights of Mother Earth) grants legal rights to water systems including Amazon tributaries — providing constitutional protection against pollution and overexploitation as part of Bolivia's unique rights-of-nature legal framework.

laws.title: Multiculturalism and Anti-Racism Law
laws.subtitle: Law 045 — Anti-Racism and Discrimination 2010
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's anti-racism law (Law 045) prohibits racial discrimination and creates the Committee Against Racism and All Forms of Discrimination (CERD Bolivia). The law criminalized media that promote racism and required decolonizing education. In practice, discrimination against indigenous peoples in employment, housing, and services remains widespread. The law was used controversially to prosecute journalists who criticized the government.
laws.penalty: Racial discrimination: 1–3 years; institutionalized racism in public entities: fines plus diversity training mandates
exceptions: Affirmative action programs for indigenous peoples are not discrimination
Cultural traditions and religious practices with discriminatory aspects under review process

quiz.q: What controversy arose from Bolivia's anti-racism Law 045?
options: It was used to prosecute journalists critical of the government
It was struck down by the courts
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's anti-racism Law 045 was used controversially to prosecute journalists who criticized the government — raising press freedom concerns that provisions against 'racist' media could become tools to silence political opposition.

laws.title: Bolivia's State of Emergency Powers
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Art. 137 — State of Exception
laws.fullDescription: Bolivia's constitution allows the President to declare a State of Exception (emergency) for 90 days (extendable once) in cases of serious internal disturbance, external threat, or natural disaster. The declaration must be approved by the Plurinational Assembly. During the 2019 crisis and COVID-19 pandemic, states of emergency were declared. Emergency powers are subject to constitutional limitations — fundamental rights like life and dignity cannot be suspended.
laws.penalty: Abuse of emergency powers beyond constitutional limits: constitutional challenge; suspension of non-derogable rights: unconstitutional
exceptions: Rights to life, dignity, and freedom from torture cannot be suspended in any emergency
International human rights obligations continue during states of exception

quiz.q: How long can Bolivia's State of Exception last under the constitution?
options: 90 days, extendable once with Assembly approval
quiz.explanation: Bolivia's constitution allows a State of Exception for 90 days, extendable once — requiring Plurinational Assembly approval and explicitly prohibiting suspension of non-derogable rights like life, dignity, and freedom from torture.
